L43: arXiv:2610.15991v1 [cs.AI] 11 Oct 2026
L44: # Revocation Is Not Complete at Receipt: An Executable Outcome Contract for Distributed Agent-Tool Gateways
L45: 
L46: Conference: The Eighth International Conference on Distributed Artificial Intelligence; November 29–December 2, 2026; Hong Kong, China The Eighth International Conference on Distributed Artificial Intelligence (DAI ’26), November 29–December 2, 2026, Hong Kong, China CCS: Security and privacy Authorization CCS: Computing methodologies Distributed artificial intelligence
L47: Lifei Liu Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Seattle, WA, USA email: lliu.lifei@gmail.com , Haoran Yu Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Seattle, WA, USA email: haoranyu889@gmail.com and Danping Zhang Affiliation: Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang, China email: zhangdanping@nchu.edu.cn
L48: 
L49: © ,
L50: ###### Abstract.
L51: 
L52: Distributed agent workflows cache delegated authority at tool gateways. Revocation may be reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence, although none of these observations establishes that all gateways enforced the change or that guarded effects stopped.
L53: We define C0–C5, a bounded outcome contract spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, and implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set, call set, and observation window. A 14-case fault matrix checks conservative classification, sticky violations, restart persistence, and evidence immutability. Treating C3 or C4 as completion produces seven or five false positives in a derived eight-case audit; the bounded C0–C5 verdict produces none.
L54: Across two separately provisioned 16-host Keycloak executions, normal delivery and recovery commit no effects, whereas receiver-selective non-delivery admits and commits 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) in every treatment block despite successful transport and receiver persistence. OPA/Toxiproxy, a live networked MCP workflow, and an unmodified closed-loop MCPMark agent reproduce the persisted-but-not-enforced boundary on narrower surfaces.
L55: In the MCPMark execution, normal C4 denies all 31 exposed post-barrier calls with no effects, whereas selective C3 allows 344 calls and commits 145 effects. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a revocation-completion verdict.
L56: ###### Keywords:
L57: 
L58: agentic AI, revocation, delegated authority, selective non-delivery, tool gateways, continuous access evaluation
L59: ## 1. Introduction
L60: Consider an agent workflow whose delegated authority is cached at eight tool gateways. A security-event transmitter sends a signed revocation to two durable receivers, each responsible for four gateways. Both receivers acknowledge and persist the event, but one receiver cannot forward it across its local control path. From the transmitter’s view, delivery succeeded; from the receiver’s view, the event is durable.
L61: The four downstream gateways nevertheless retain the stale authority and can still commit Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects. This is the failure isolated by E-B24: in every treatment block, receiver B returns HTTP 202 and stores the event while its four gateways admit all 112 calls assigned to them. The example exposes the question at the center of this paper: when may a distributed agent system declare revocation complete?
L62: Prior work provides substantial machinery for moving and recording revocation state. Agent-authorization proposals specify signed notifications, retries, status fallback, descendant invalidation, authoritative logs, heartbeat expiry, gossip, and evidence records  (【32†Singla, 2026】; 【33†Cruz, 2026】; 【34†Kumar, 2026】; 【35†Nelson, 2026】; 【36†Deochake, 2026】). OAuth token revocation already recognizes that some servers may learn an invalidation later than others (【37†Lodderstedt et al., 2013】).
L63: Global Token Revocation distinguishes a successful revocation request from revocation completion and permits an optional completion notification  (【38†Parecki, 2026】). Its completion condition concerns issuer-side token revocation and reauthentication; it does not require receipts from a distributed gateway population or effect-side observations.
L64: CAEP and the Shared Signals Framework (SSF) define security events and PUSH or POLL delivery between transmitters and receivers  (【39†Cappalli and Tulshibagwale, 2025】; 【40†Tulshibagwale et al., 2025】); permit receipts move authorization evidence closer to an effect boundary (【41†Lee, 2026】). Proof of Execution separates authorization, enforcement, effects, and records, while Notarized Agents obtains receiver-attested action receipts  (【42†Rhodes and Kang, 2026】; 【43†Figuera, 2026】).
L65: These systems address complementary objects. Issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, receiver persistence, gateway enforcement, and effect prevention remain distinct facts. Evaluating only the earlier stages can hide a stale gateway; evaluating only denied calls can hide fail-closed availability loss; and a modeled propagation result does not establish that real tool effects stopped.
L66: We study revocation completion as an end-to-end, bounded outcome rather than as a property of a particular propagation mechanism. The research question is: what evidence is sufficient to certify that a declared set of agent-tool gateways enforced a revocation and prevented a declared set of effects during a finite observation window? We separate the path into C0–C5: issuer commit, transmitter queueing, transport acknowledgment, receiver persistence, gateway enforcement, and effect prevention.

L49: # When Does Authorization End? Effect Closure at Provider Boundaries
L50: 
L51: Igor Santos-Grueiro Affiliation: International University of La Rioja
L52: igor.santosgrueiro@unir.net
L53: ###### Abstract
L54: 
L55: Revocation completion, clean state, or operation success can leave authorized work able to cause an effect the application rejects while the provider stays within its contract. We call the absence of all such paths policy-relative effect closure, or effect closure for short. Thus, a grant is closed when its existing authorizations retain no such path, and it cannot issue any new ones.
L56: We present EffectBound, which uses an evidence-supported finite contract to decide whether an interface can truthfully report closure while required work completes. It reduces this to finite control with hidden state and returns a strategy, an impossibility certificate, or no verdict when evidence is insufficient. Machine-checked proofs establish the reduction and checker soundness; the checker derives closure results and validates certificates.
L57: Across GitHub, Kubernetes, NATS, and Kafka, closure fails in three ways: an interface lacks a needed control, clean visible state hides active work, or the model stops before the effect frontier—the last point where the effect can be prevented. The GitHub tool cannot bind a merge to the reviewed commit; a controlled run confirms that it may merge a different commit. NATS can report no stored or pending messages while dispatched work can still publish downstream.
L58: In Kafka, all fixed-set brokers had applied the revocation, yet an earlier authorized request could still append. We add a gate that blocks new use of revoked authority and delays return until earlier in-flight work completes. In a fixed-set Kafka 4.3.1 test deployment, this closes the studied synchronous, nontransactional write path without blocking unrelated requests. For a grant, authorization ends only when issuance stops and no earlier authorization can reach an effect the application rejects.
L59: ## I Introduction
L60: When can a provider boundary truthfully report that previously authorized work can no longer cause an effect the application rejects? We trace six paths from authorization to application effect in GitHub, Kubernetes, NATS, and Kafka. Consider an application using GitHub’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to merge pull request 42. The application approves $h_{1}$ and calls merge_pull_request, but the head may move to $h_{2}$ before merge.
L61: GitHub’s native API [【37†1】] can reject the merge if the head no longer matches the reviewed commit, whereas the tested MCP tool [【38†2】] exposes no equivalent check. Reads may all return $h_{1}$, yet the head can change after the last one. Refusing or reading forever blocks required work; proceeding without a condition may merge $h_{2}$. Thus, a component limited to this MCP interface cannot guarantee both safety and completion, although both interfaces behave as documented.
L62: The MCP interface reaches the effect but cannot bind it to the reviewed commit.
L63: We found a different failure in Kafka: a model can end too early. Our initial model allowed return after every broker in the declared fixed set applied the access control list (ACL) deletion [【39†3】, 【40†4】]. We paused a request after authorization, yet it appended after return: authorizer convergence was real, but the model stopped before the effect frontier at append.
L64: We therefore designed Effect Fence: it blocks new use of revoked authority and delays return until earlier in-flight work completes, extending closure to append. A correct proof can stop before the effect frontier: verification is only as meaningful as the effect path it reaches.
L65: We model both failures along $g\rightarrow a\rightarrow c\rightarrow F\rightarrow e$: grant lineage $g$ issues authorization instance $a$; continuation $c$ carries it; and effect $e$ follows the last preventable point $F$, the effect frontier. The chain distinguishes future-use closure, instance-effect closure, and quiescence (all work stopping). We argue that authorization ends for a lineage only when no new instance can be issued and no previously issued instance retains a path to a rejected effect.
L66: We call the second condition policy-relative effect closure, or effect closure for short. It is distinct from local completion and quiescence: safe work may continue.
L67: This is not only a check/use problem. In NATS [【41†5】, 【42†6】] and Kafka, authorized work can still cause effects after a local completion signal; Kubernetes [【43†7】] adds post-authorization mutation and already-admitted requests. The six paths span late-bound names, post-check state changes, admitted execution, repeated delivery, callbacks, and distributed in-flight work. Each shows how issued authority can still cause an effect.
L68: We selected them for structural diversity rather than to estimate prevalence.
L69: Prior work studies revocation and ongoing use, check/use and authorization–execution divergence, and enforcement over supplied interfaces or models [【44†8】, 【45†9】, 【46†10】, 【47†11】, 【48†12】, 【49†13】]. Commit-time authorization [【50†14】] rechecks authority at an exposed commit point.
L70: In contrast, we present EffectBound, which uses a finite contract constructed from provider evidence to decide whether the provider boundary reaches the effect frontier and exposes enough control to close rejected paths while required work completes. It returns a strategy, a losing certificate, or Unsupported when evidence is insufficient. We contribute policy-relative effect-closure semantics, frontier adequacy, and boundary realizability.
